newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Weaker Slovak crown needed for better C/A-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Weaker Slovak crown needed for better C/A-analysts.

text.p: Slovakia's current account deficit widened to $479 million in the first quarter of 1997 from $420 million in the same period of 1996, and analysts said the situation would not improve without a weaker crown.
"The trade deficit, which is crucial for the current account figures, could improve definitely with a cheaper crown," Vladimir Kuklis of Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka (CSOB) told Reuters.
"An immediate small drop (of the crown) would be definitely better than a possible deep fall later," he added.
The Slovak central bank (NBS) has been squeezing crown liquidity in order to prevent foreign speculators from borrowing crowns on long positions to sell on spot.
As a result, the interbank market remains around 34 percent short of funds needed to meet minimum reserve requirements and money market rates remain extremely high.
On Friday, average overnight interbank rates were quoted at 30 percent on the bid and 80 percent on the offer side.
The NBS moves have kept the crown steady in recent days at around 33.5 to the dollar and 19.4 to the mark, implying a deviation from the mid-point of its mark/dollar basket of minus 0.6 percent.

Despite the current stability of the crown, Kuklis said devaluation expectations, driven by fears of a knock-on effect from the fall of the Czech crown, could have encouraged some Slovak companies to make foreign payments in advance.
Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said the current account deficit could be made worse by the decline of the Czech crown even if it did not prompt copy-cat speculative selling of the Slovak currency.
"The Czech crown is cheaper now, which could open the way for Czech importers to capture the Slovak market," Briska said.
Slovakia is already running a near two billion crown trade deficit with the Czech Republic, which accounts for around a quarter of its total trade turnover.

The analysts said that even though the visible trade deficit for the first quarter fell to $477.2 million from $514.8 million in the first quarter of 1996, the overall level of the deficit was worryingly high.
"These figures indicate that the situation will not change for the better pretty soon," Libor Briska from Bratislava branch of Creditanstalt said.
Despite both analysts' calls for a depreciation to help the trade deficit, neither thought the NBS was likely to move in that direction in the near future.
"The government and the National Bank (NBS) have several possible measures, including devaluation, to help this to reverse, but so far we don't see any action", he said.

On Friday, NBS vice governor Marian Jusko told a national newspaper that an imminent speculative attack on the crown was unlikely in the near future and that speculators betting on a devaluation would lose money.
